# Defining High Confidence Targets of Differential CpG Methylation in Response to In Utero Arsenic Exposure and Implications for Cancer Risk

**Authors:** Tabitha Lumour-Mensah; Bernardo Lemos

**Affiliations:** 1.Department of Environmental Health, Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA | 2.R. Ken Coit College of Pharmacy, The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ

## Abstract

Arsenic is a relatively abundant metalloid that impacts DNA methylation and has been implicated in various adverse health outcomes including several cancers and diabetes. However, uncertainty remains about the identity of genomic CpGs that are sensitive to arsenic exposure, in utero or otherwise. Here we identified a high confidence set of CpG sites whose methylation is sensitive to in utero arsenic exposure. To do so, we analyzed methylation of infant CpGs as a function of maternal urinary arsenic in cord blood and placenta from geographically and ancestrally distinct human populations. Independent analyses of these distinct populations were followed by combination of results across sexes and populations/tissue types. Following these analyses, we concluded that both sex and tissue type are important drivers of heterogeneity in methylation response at several CpGs. We also identified 17 high confidence CpGs that were hypermethylated across sex, tissue type and population; 11 of these were located within protein coding genes. This pattern is consistent with hypotheses that arsenic increases cancer risk by inducing the hypermethylation of genic regions. This study represents an opportunity to understand consistent, reproducible patterns of epigenomic responses after in utero arsenic exposure and may aid towards novel biomarkers or signatures of arsenic exposure. Identifying arsenic-responsive sites can also contribute to our understanding of the biological mechanisms by which arsenic exposure can affect biological function and increase risk of cancer and other age-related diseases.

## Introduction

Arsenic is a relatively abundant metalloid that has been implicated in several adverse health outcomes including skin lesions, elevated risk of diabetes, pulmonary disfunction, cardiovascular disease, and cancers at various exposure levels (De Loma et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2021; Lai et al., 1994; Marciniak et al., 2020; Moon et al., 2012; Parvez et al., 2013; M. Rahman et al., 2006; Su et al., 2022). Despite this, arsenic exposure can occur via inhalation as well as via the drinking water of populations in various regions and countries around the world. Arsenic in drinking water often occurs at levels that exceed the 10 ppb maximum contaminant level (MCL) that has been designated by the World Health Organization as an acceptable level for consumption. For example, while the current Mexican MCL for arsenic in drinking water is 25 ppb, residents of certain areas such as the Gómez Palacio region are believed to have been exposed to levels as high as 50 ppb (Laine et al., 2015). Similarly, certain US populations including those in some parts of New Hampshire that consume unregulated well water in areas with high geogenic arsenic are also at risk of high arsenic exposure (Green et al., 2016a; Lombard et al., 2021). Further, arsenic toxicity has been observed at doses currently classified as low or moderate, indicating that exposure to even amounts below this 10 ppb threshold considered acceptable by current regulatory standards may still pose risk to human health (Chen et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2020; Nuvolone et al., 2023).

Approximately 70–90% of arsenic ingested through drinking water or food is readily absorbed and enters the bloodstream, with variability depending on the arsenic species ingested and biological factors of the exposed individual (Palma-Lara et al., 2019). Once in the bloodstream, arsenic ingested during gestation can pass into and through the placenta to accumulate in newborn and fetal tissues, thus supporting the need to evaluate the consequences of arsenic during fetal development (Bulka et al., 2022; Devesa et al., 2006; Markowski et al., 2011). Relatedly, in utero arsenic exposure has been associated with various adverse infant/child outcomes including detriments in visual-spatial reasoning, memory, language, increased risk of ADHD, spina bifida, low birthweight, pulmonary disease and attenuated immune function during childhood, and all-cause childhood mortality (Farzan et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2020; M. Rahman et al., 2013; M. L. Rahman et al., 2017; Raqib et al., 2009; Signes-Pastor et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2006; Tindula et al., 2021; Tyler & Allan, 2014; Vahter et al., 2020). Thus, arsenic exposure remains a highly relevant environmental health concern, given the toxicity of this metalloid, the multiple routes of exposure, its high uptake in the body, the relative abundance of the element, and the fact that there are several populations exposed to airborne arsenic containing particulate matter as well as to high arsenic concentrations in drinking water across the globe.

Previous studies have suggested that arsenic exposure in utero may cause epigenetic alterations and impact downstream health outcomes (Cardenas et al., 2015; Green et al., 2016b; Koestler et al., 2013; Rojas et al., 2015; Winterbottom et al., 2019). Notably, sex has emerged as an important modifier of the relationship between arsenic exposure and the epigenome (Nohara et al., 2011; Winterbottom et al., 2019). However, defining a set of high confidence arsenic-sensitive CpGs has remained a challenge, with human population studies reporting different sets of CpGs, different numbers of CpGs, and different magnitudes of effect. This variability is likely to be partially due to differences in sample population, exposure dose, sex, tissue of analyses, experimental methods, analytical methods, and in some cases reporting of only the most statistically significant sites within a given study.

In this study, we combine data from two distinct datasets evaluating DNA methylation in different tissues of newborns with varying levels of in utero arsenic exposure. Our goal is to identify specific CpGs that are preferentially methylated or demethylated in response to in utero arsenic exposure in a consistent manner across populations, tissues, and arsenic exposure concentrations.

## Materials and Methods

### Sample Populations and Data Sources

All arsenic exposure and epigenetic data analyzed in this study were publicly available data accessed through the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database managed by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) under GEO accession numbers GSE71678 and GSE62924. Briefly, this data was drawn from two separate epidemiological cohorts: the New Hampshire Birth Cohort Study (NHBCS) and the Biomarkers of Exposure to Arsenic (BEAR) birth cohort.

#### New Hampshire Birth cohort study (GSE71678)

Descriptions of the New Hampshire Birth Cohort Study (NHBCS) are detailed in more depth elsewhere by the original investigators of this study (Green et al., 2016a; Punshon et al., 2015). In brief, the sample population is composed of 343 mother-infant pairs with known arsenic exposure due to use of contaminated well-water in New Hampshire, USA. Arsenic exposure was measured in maternal toenails collected within 8 weeks post-partum, urine samples collected at 24–28 weeks of gestation and fetal-side placental tissues obtained after delivery. DNA methylation of the infants born to these mothers was measured in placental tissue retrieved post-delivery using the Illumina 450K BeadChip array (Punshon et al., 2015).

#### Biomarkers of Exposure to Arsenic birth cohort (GSE62924)

Descriptions of the Biomarkers of Exposure to ARsenic (BEAR) birth cohort are detailed in more depth elsewhere by the original investigators of this study (Rojas et al., 2015). In summary, the study set is a composed of 38 mother-infant pairs recruited in Gómez Palacio, Mexico – a region with known naturally-occurring arsenic contamination of groundwater. Arsenic exposure was measured in maternal urine collected at time of delivery and drinking water sources (municipal or commercially packaged) measured within four weeks of newborn delivery. Further, DNA methylation was measured in newborn cord blood using the Illumina 450K BeadChip array (Illumina, San Diego, CA) (Rager et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2015).

### Statistical Analyses

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.1. Broadly, analysis methods were standardized across both populations to maximize comparability of findings. In all analyses, the limma package was employed to fit linear regression models in which CpG methylation was modeled as a function of continuous arsenic exposure (Ritchie et al., 2015). For analysis of both populations, total maternal inorganic urinary arsenic concentration will be the proxy exposure of in utero arsenic. Using total maternal inorganic urinary arsenic concentration as the main predictor, maximizes comparability in exposure metric across these two populations.

Infant outcomes such as birthweight were not included in models to avoid the potential for collider stratification bias. However, there was a relatively high number of smokers (n=42), a likely confounder of gestational arsenic exposure and DNA methylation, in the US population when compared to the number of smokers in the Mexico-based population (n=1) so this covariate was controlled for in analyses of the US data.

In addition, sex has been demonstrated to be a consistent modifier of the effect of arsenic on DNA methylation and several health outcomes including childhood neurodevelopment, tumor development and lung function (Broberg et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2020; Pilsner et al., 2012; Ramsey et al., 2013; Waalkes et al., 2003; Winterbottom et al., 2019). To account for the role of infant sex as an effect measure modifier of the relationship between arsenic exposure and DNA methylation, all analyses will be stratified by infant sex.

While sex-stratified analyses were conducted separately for each population, results were combined to find a set of shared sites across populations. In order to find this set of CpGs consistently hyper- or hypomethylated across both populations, we combined P-values adjusted for multiple testing using the Holm-Bonferroni correction across both analyses using the Fisher P-value combination method with an FDR of 5% using the fishercomb R function (Rau et al., 2014).

## Results

### Characteristics of Study Populations

The mean birthweight for was 3.26 kilograms (sd 0.505) for infants in the Mexico-based population and 3.44 kilograms (sd = 0.511) for infants in the US population. In addition, the average age at time of pregnancy was higher in the US population than the Mexico population (Table 1). In general, arsenic exposure was higher in the Mexico-based population than the US-based population (Figure 1) (Xu et al., 2021). Mean arsenic levels measured in maternal urine collected during pregnancy were 67.40 μg/L (sd = 78.90) in mothers from the Mexican population and 5.63 μg/L (sd = 10.77) in mothers from the US population (Table 1). In addition, mean arsenic levels did not vary significantly between mothers to males and mothers to females neither within the Mexican population (P-value = 0.1965) nor within the US population (P value = 0.369).

### Differentially Methylated CpGs

Given the documented role of sex as an effect measure modifier of the relationship between arsenic and CpG methylation, differential methylation analyses were conducted separately in male and female infants (Nohara et al., 2011; Winterbottom et al., 2019). Modeling CpG methylation as a function of increasing arsenic exposure, we identified statistically significant associations in both populations. Specifically, we identified 470 CpGs that were statistically significant after correction for multiple testing within female infants from the Mexico population (adjusted P value < 0.055) with 326 of these CpGs located within annotated genes. However, no CpG was significantly differentially methylated as a function of maternal urinary arsenic in male infants of the Mexican population (Figure 2). In female infants of the US population, 1,527 CpGs were significantly differentially methylated (adjusted P value < 0.055) as a function of increasing maternal urinary arsenic with 1,338 of these localized within genes. In addition, 987 CpGs were significantly differentially methylated (adjusted P value < 0.055) as a function of maternal urinary arsenic in male infants, with 800 of these located within genes (Figure 3).

### Shared CpGs Across Males and Females within Each Population

We did not find any overlapping CpGs or genes across sexes in the Mexico population given the lack of sites maintaining statistical significance after correction for multiple testing in males in the Mexico-based population. However, 19 CpGs within the US population were hypermethylated in both males and females (adjusted P value < 0.055). (Supplemental Table i).

### Shared CpGs and Genes Across both Sex and Tissues in Both Populations

Within females, one CpG (cg09423703) was statistically significantly hypermethylated in separate analyses of both the US and Mexican populations (Table 2). This CpG is located within a CpG island on chromosome 2 (chr2:71114733-71115474). Additionally, 20 genes were implicated in both cohorts of female infants (Table 3). Of these, MAD1L1, BAT2, and FBRSL1 had more than one differentially methylated CpG in at least one of the two populations. MAD1L1 is a member of the mitotic spindle-assembly checkpoint responsible for preventing the onset of anaphase until chromosomes are in position in the metaphase plate. Dysfunction of this gene is associated with tumorigenesis. Further, polymorphisms in this gene are associated with increased risk of chromosomal abnormalities in fetuses (Chan et al., 2023). FBRSL1 has been linked to RNA binding, however the exact function of this gene is not completely characterized. However, polymorphisms in AUTS2, a paralog of FBRSL1 have been associated with an intellectual disability syndrome with microcephaly on the autism spectrum of disorders (Pauli et al., 2021).

In females, of all CpGs included in this analysis, we note that 63,635 CpGs had concordant negative fold changes in both populations and 112,152 CpGs had concordant positive fold changes in both populations. On the other hand, 108,234 CpGs had positive fold change in the US population and negative fold change in the Mexico population, whereas 60,307 CpGs had negative fold changes in the US population and positive fold changes in the Mexico population. After combining p-values of concordant CpGs in female infants across both populations, we identified thirty-six differentially methylated CpGs (adjusted P value < 0.055). Of these, two CpGs were significantly hypomethylated in both populations and thirty-four CpGs were significantly hypermethylated in females of both populations (Table 4).

In males, of all CpGs included in this analysis, 70,166 CpGs had concordant negative fold changes in both populations and 97,713 CpGs had concordant positive fold changes in both populations. On the other hand, 105,467 CpGs had positive fold change in the US population and negative fold change in the Mexican population, whereas 70,982 CpGs had negative fold changes in the US population and positive fold changes in the Mexican population. After combining p-values of concordant CpGs in male infants across both populations, we identified 40 differentially methylated CpGs (adjusted P value < 0.055). Of these, four CpGs were significantly hypomethylated and thirty-six CpGs were significantly hypermethylated in males of both populations (Table 5).

### High Confidence CpGs Across Tissues and Sex

Finally, to assess the strength of the evidence of common CpG targets for arsenic exposure, consider infant sexes, and include information across tissue/population in one analysis, we combined P values across all four associations (female-infant cord blood, male-infant cord blood, female-infant placenta and male-infant placenta). Our analyses identified 17 CpGs that were consistently hypermethylated when both sexes and tissues were combined across the two populations; 11 of these CpGs were located within genes. However, there were no sites that were consistently hypomethylated when both sexes and tissues were combined across the two populations (Table 6).

### High confidence CpGs across sexes and tissues/populations

Sex-specific direction of effect was still observed after P value combination across sexes and tissues of the two populations. Accordingly, seven CpGs were hypermethylated in one sex and hypomethylated in the other, with five of these seven CpGs located within genes. Furthermore, tissue type/population specific variation in the direction of effect was also observed. Thirteen CpGs were hypermethylated in one population/tissue type and hypomethylated in the other, eleven of which are located within genes. Finally, there were twenty-nine CpGs (twenty-four of which are associated with genes) that were hypermethylated in all but one stratum of analysis and ten CpGs (nine of which are associated with genes) that were hypomethylated in all but one population (Figure 4; Supplemental figure i).

## Discussion

The primary goal of this study was to identify specific CpGs that are sensitive to arsenic exposure in individuals exposed to arsenic during gestation. To address this question, DNA methylation was evaluated at cytosine residues in DNA extracted from infant tissues. By utilizing maternal arsenic levels in urine during pregnancy as a proxy for gestational arsenic exposure in infants and DNA extracted from two different types of fetal tissue in two separate populations, we can identify reproducible epigenetic response to gestational arsenic exposure in a way that is not limited to one specific tissue, sex, or population. Ultimately, our analyses implicated seventeen CpGs that were consistently hypermethylated across infant sex, tissue-type and study population.

Given that DNA methylation is an important mechanism for the regulation of cellular function, identifying targets of arsenic exposure can advance our understanding of the mechanisms by which arsenic exposure confers increases risk of several downstream health outcomes. For example, previous work has indicated that arsenic can induce hypermethylation, and that hypermethylation of certain genes such as tumor suppressor genes can be associated with a variety of cancers (C. Chen et al., 2022; He et al., 2019; Kulis & Esteller, 2010; Lu et al., 2014; Rauluseviciute et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). Conversely, global DNA methylation loss has also been suggested in DNA repeats upon arsenic exposure. Loss of arsenic in these regions could be linked with genomic instability which can also lead to tumorigenesis (Greenberg & Bourc’his, 2019; Guo et al., 2023; Kulis & Esteller, 2010; Zhang et al., 2023). Thus, the collective evidence indicates roles for both hyper- and hypo- methylation in arsenic-induced cancers, and the identification of sensitive sites and regions remain critical.

In both cord blood and placenta extracted from female infants increasing gestational arsenic levels were associated with changes in DNA methylation. In cord blood from infants born in Gómez Palacio (Mexico), 470 CpGs were significantly differentially methylated in response to increasing arsenic exposure. In addition, 1,527 CpGs were significantly differentially methylated in fetal side placental tissues collected from a New Hampshire-based population (USA). Unlike their female counterparts, the cord blood taken from male infants born in Gómez Palacio, did not demonstrate any statistically significant difference in DNA methylation as a function of arsenic exposure. However, the DNA methylation in placental tissues taken from male infants born in New Hampshire did vary as a function of gestation arsenic exposure with 987 CpGs being statistically significantly associated with arsenic exposure level. While considering these tissues and populations separately, nineteen CpGs were differentially methylated in placental tissues taken from females. When expanding our analysis to include whole genes rather than individual CpGs, we found twenty common genes across populations that had at least one differentially methylated CpG within the gene itself.

P value combination analysis is one method to integrate data across both populations and tissue types, and demonstrated that there is a set of CpGs that are statistically significant despite differences in tissue type and study population. After using Fisher’s method of p-value combination to leverage information for females and males separately across study populations, there were 36 CpGs that were either hypomethylated or hypermethylated in females of both populations and 40 CpGs that were either hypomethylated or hypermethylated in males of both populations. Interestingly, in females, one of these higher confidence CpGs identified in both tissues/populations (cg23992410) is located within the PROX1 gene. This gene codes for a transcription factor that binds DNA and plays a key role in embryonic development. More specifically, it functions as an important regulatory protein in neurogenesis, heart, eye, liver, pancreas and lymphatic development (Elsir et al., 2012; Miyoshi et al., 2015; Wigle & Oliver, 1999). While none of the CpGs of high confidence in males were located within the PROX1 gene, one of these CpGs was located within IRX3, a protein that plays a role in neural development during gestation (Bright et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2022; Moazeny et al., 2022). Similarly, another CpG is located within EBF2, a gene in the COE family of proteins that play important role in a variety of developmental processes including bone formation (Nieminen-Pihala et al., 2022). BMP3, another gene related to bone formation, was also associated with four CpGs. BMP3 encodes transcription factors that suppresses osteoblast differentiation and bone density (Daluiski et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2010).

Given the likely role of arsenic in several cancers, it is important to consider whether any of the genes associated with these high confidence CpGs have also been implicated in cancer (Cheng et al., 2016; De Loma et al., 2020; Kozono et al., 2018). For example, one of the 17 high confidence CpG across sex and tissue was HSPH1, a gene that encodes a protein that plays a role in the aggregation of misfolded proteins, is overexpressed in several tumor types and has been found to bind with inorganic arsenic (Dong et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020). Relatedly, two of the twenty high confidence CpGs in females (cg02318347 and cg03373442) were within HSPH1. Another cancer-related gene for which a high confidence CpG was found was BMP3. BMP3 has been associated with various cancers and hypermethylation of this gene has been documented to be a reliable biomarker for colorectal cancer (X. R. Chen et al., 2010; Kisiel et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2019). In addition, in males, BMP3 was a gene in which four high confidence CpGs (cg20642710, cg22403273, cg26105156, cg26917673) were found. Further, some of the sex-specific genes have also been associated with cancer. Specifically, one of our high-confidence CpG-associated genes in females (PROX1) has been associated with breast cancers (Zhu et al., 2022).

It is important to note that there are limitations of this study. First, there are limitations in tissue availability in these populations due to their focus on newborns without major health concerns that would necessitate surgical intervention. Consequently, our findings about a set of high confidence CpGs should be qualified by our lack of data in any tissue type outside of cord blood and placenta. However, the possibility of expanding these analyses to other tissue types as more studies are conducted on the relationship between in utero arsenic exposure and DNA methylation in newborns may present a promising step forward in this research. A second limitation in this study is that it is probable that we have not completely controlled for all sources of confounding. However, due to the design of this study, confounding would only be a concern if the potential confounding factor was so in both populations. Another limitation is that we have extrapolated one metric for arsenic exposure at one time to exposure throughout gestation. It is important to note that arsenic exposure can vary due to behavioral changes, dietary changes, and changes in water use as well as natural temporal changes in arsenic concentration in groundwater sources themselves (Calderon et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2022). In addition, timing of exposure may have an important role in the effects of arsenic on the epigenome due to the precise temporal nature of fetal development (Schoenwolf et al., 2021). Finally, a forth limitation is that folate levels were not considered, but it may also be an effect measure modifier of the impact of arsenic exposure on DNA methylation as well as newborn health outcomes associated with arsenic exposure (Crider et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2019). While, lack of data about maternal folate levels prevents analyses of these potential impacts, we note that this confounding would only be a concern here if it were so in both populations.

Despite this, there are notable strengths associated with our approach in this study. One strength is that standardizing analyses and combining results from separate but otherwise identical analyses allows for more accurate assessment of reproducibility and CpGs sensitivity to arsenic. The more common approach of conducting an analysis within one population and commenting on any similarities in reported sites in past studies is also a useful approach. However, these may be harder to interpret and not fully equipped to capture important findings across studies due to differences in how complete lists from these previous studies are and inability to pool data across studies. Heterogeneity in analytical approach across studies is another major limitation that our approach circumvents. Overall, the analyses highlight the critical importance of data sharing and data deposition to public repositories with unfettered data access that enable data integration.

Importantly, this study is the first to our knowledge that attempts to establish a set of CpGs that are uniquely sensitive to arsenic exposure during development in distinct but related tissues in separate populations. However, it is important for future studies to include more populations and tissues to establish a more complete list of high confidence CpGs. Establishing a robust set of high confidence CpGs will further our understanding of the scope of health outcomes associated with gestational arsenic exposure as well as the biological mechanisms underlying these effects. Further, this work opens the door for the potential establishment of CpG-based biomarkers in infants whose direct arsenic exposure cannot be reasonably measured by traditional methods.

## Conclusions

This study represents the first attempt to establish a set of high-confidence CpG targets for gestational arsenic exposure. The establishment of these seventeen high-confidence sites represents a step towards advancing our understanding of the biological mechanisms of effect of in utero exposure to arsenic on development and downstream health outcomes such as cancer. In addition, further exploration of this approach presents the opportunity to establish a novel biomarker for arsenic exposure in infants whose previous exposure cannot otherwise be measured directly.
